test_title: PYST 61: SSC CGL 2024 - Quantitative Aptitude (Held On 17 Sept, 2024 Shift 1)
subject: maths
question: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 15 hours and 25 hours, respectively, whereas pipe C can empty the full tank in 40 hours. All three pipes are opened together, but pipe A is closed after 5 hours. After how many hours will the remaining part of the tank be filled?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Total capacity (LCM of 15, 25, 40) = 600 units.

Efficiencies: A = 40, B = 24, C = −15 units/hr.

Work done in first 5 hours = 5 × (40 + 24 − 15) = 245 units.

Remaining work = 600 − 245 = 355 units.

Time to fill remaining part by B and C = 355 ÷ (24 − 15) = 355 ÷ 9 = 39 ⁴/₉ hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 39 ⁴/₉ hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

⇒ Time taken by pipe A to fill the tank = 15 hours

⇒ Time taken by pipe B to fill the tank = 25 hours

⇒ Time taken by pipe C to empty the tank = 40 hours

⇒ All three pipes are opened together for 5 hours before A is closed.

**Calculations:**

⇒ Combined efficiency of A, B, and C = 40 + 24 − 15 = 49 units/hr

⇒ Total work done by all three pipes in 5 hours = 49 × 5 = 245 units

⇒ Remaining work to be completed = 600 − 245 = 355 units

⇒ After 5 hours, pipe A is closed. Thus, the remaining work is done by pipes B and C.

⇒ Combined efficiency of pipes B and C = 24 − 15 = 9 units/hr

⇒ Time required by B and C to fill the remaining tank = 355 ÷ 9 = 39 ⁴/₉ hours

**∴ The correct answer is 39 ⁴/₉ hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Pipes and Cisterns Concept

If a pipe can fill a tank in *x* hours, its efficiency is 1/x of the tank per hour. If a pipe empties the tank in *y* hours, its efficiency is −1/y per hour.

Total Work using LCM

Taking the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of the given times as the total capacity of the tank avoids complex fraction calculations and directly gives individual efficiencies in integer units.

Negative Efficiency

Any pipe or leak that empties a cistern performs negative work. Its efficiency is assigned a minus sign and must be algebraically added to the efficiencies of the filling pipes to find the net work rate.
